title: Artificial Intelligence: Council and Parliament agree to simplify and streamline rules
date_evidence: On May 7, 2026, the Council presidency and European Parliament negotiators reached a provisional agreement on a proposal to streamline certain rules regarding artificial intelligence (AI). The proposal forms part of the so-called 'Omnibus VII' legislative package.
key_claim: On 7 May 2026 the Council presidency and European Parliament reached a provisional agreement on the AI Omnibus (part of the seventh 'Omnibus' simplification package), postponing high-risk AI obligations and watermarking deadlines and streamlining the AI Act while framing the change as simplification.
notes: Tier 1 primary; the co-legislators' agreement. Page is JS-rendered and did not yield body via fetch; date captured from WebSearch snippet and the dated URL path /2026/05/07/, corroborated by the European Parliament release and Taylor Wessing citation.

title: AI Act: deal on simplification measures, ban on "nudifier" apps
date_evidence: Press release 07-05-2026 - 05:06 20260427IPR42011 AI Act: deal on simplification measures, ban on “nudifier” apps
key_claim: Parliament and Council postponed high-risk AI obligations to 2 December 2027 (high-risk use cases) and 2 August 2028 (AI as safety components in regulated products) and watermarking to 2 December 2026; added an EU ban on nudifier apps and AI-generated CSAM; narrowed 'safety component', carved out machinery, and extended SME exemptions to small mid-caps, while stating the deal maintains the Act's 'main provisions and risk-based approach'.
verbatim_quote: maintaining its main provisions and risk-based approach
notes: Tier 1 co-legislator press release; concrete postponed deadlines and scope changes.

title: Is the Brussels Effect Fading?
key_claim: The Digital Omnibus proposes to pause implementation of the AI Act and revise data-protection rules; a 'Washington Pull' (including US Commerce Secretary Lutnick tying steel/aluminium tariff relief to the EU softening the DSA/DMA) is moving the EU closer to the US regulatory orbit, with recent developments suggesting the Brussels Effect is slowly disappearing.
notes: Single structural anchor (3 December 2025, ~180 days): the canonical 'Brussels Effect fading' framing source for the signal.

title: The EU's Digital Omnibus is heading in the wrong direction
date_evidence: Policy 30.03.2026 The EU's Digital Omnibus is heading in the wrong direction Policy Brief
key_claim: The Digital and AI Omnibus are presented as technical simplification but propose substantive changes advanced without impact assessments; part of von der Leyen's competitiveness agenda (ten omnibus packages in 2025, a 'digital fitness check' planned for Q1 2027, a 25% admin-burden cut target by 2030), the package risks entrenching foreign big tech and undermining the EU's digital-sovereignty and competitiveness goals.
notes: Tier 2 think-tank; structural framing of simplification as a standing deregulatory mode and the sovereignty/big-tech risk.

title: What the EU AI Omnibus Deal Changes for the AI Act and What Lies Ahead
key_claim: The AI Omnibus, underpinned by the Draghi Report and industry demand, postponed high-risk obligations chiefly because harmonised standards were not finalised (a situation 'widely deemed unworkable for industry'); the core requirements 'remain substantively unchanged', and the AI Omnibus is 'only a precursor' to a GDPR/Data Omnibus with far more far-reaching implications for AI and fundamental rights.
notes: Tier 3 high-quality analysis (Laura Caroli, former senior policy advisor); supplies the standards-capacity mechanism, the Draghi driver, and the counter-point that core obligations are unchanged.

title: The EU Digital Omnibus on AI – What the political deal means
key_claim: The deal responds to 'delayed standards, unclear governance and heavier-than-expected compliance costs'; industry groups (CCIA Europe, Business Software Alliance) say it falls short of meaningful simplification, and the TÜV Association warns the machinery 'sector exit' could create regulatory fragmentation, legal uncertainty and more rather than less bureaucracy while slowing industrial-AI standards.
notes: Tier 3 law-firm analysis; concrete deadline changes and the fragmentation critique.

title: AI Omnibus: Reject the proposals to undermine transparency in the AI Act
key_claim: Sixty civil-society organisations, including EDRi, warn that exempting AI providers from registering systems they self-declare as not high-risk (deleting Article 49(2)) would risk 'transforming the AI Act into a form of self-regulation', weakening enforcement and fundamental-rights protection for a saving the Commission estimates at about EUR 100 per company.
verbatim_quote: transforming the AI Act into a form of self-regulation
notes: Tier 4 advocacy (stated position); the contested civil-society view on the magnitude of the rollback. Treat directionally.
